claims.text: The target material is initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Controlled heating and cooling will be used to study the particles' thermal response.
Rapid cooling maintains a high-entropy state at room temperature.
Premelting and melting behavior is governed by an interplay among chemical complexity, nanoscale phase-transition behavior, and varied particle configurations.
A stochastic particle-formation model can explain the premelting and melting behavior.
Stochastic principles govern the formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Limited precursor mobility favors single-phase HEA nanoparticle formation.
Increasing the number of atom types under limited mobility makes random-alloy formation more likely.
The heating and cooling treatment will produce a single-phase Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticle.
The resulting particle will exhibit uniform elemental mixing.
The resulting particle will have a diameter below 5 nm.
Bulk high-entropy-alloy material is the baseline comparator.
The hypothesis is limited to a high-entropy state retained at room temperature through rapid cooling.
Joule heating of amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors is an appropriate experiment for testing the proposed premelting and melting mechanism.
Failure of nanoparticles to form and stabilize on carbon supports would falsify the proposed premelting and melting mechanism.
Failure of amorphous carbon fibers to crystallize into T-graphite would falsify the proposed HEA premelting and melting mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns premelting and melting of initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles, whereas the proposed falsification experiment begins with metal precursors on carbon and primarily tests nanoparticle formation and support crystallization.
Rapid cooling is asserted to be essential for retaining the high-entropy state, but the falsification design specifies Joule heating without a defined cooling step or cooling-rate comparison.
